doc.title: Adrian Cunningham interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 31, 2021

title: Sounding American and 'improvised music' in Australia
summary: They discuss whether Australians aim to sound American, jazz as fundamentally American music, and Australian groups calling it 'improvised music'.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: It is. Rossano Sportiello said something once to me that really made an impression on me when he was in his late teens learning to play, much like you were I think in clubs and stuff, and if they had a particularly good night he said that would say to one another, “You were wonderful tonight, you sounded American.” And I wonder if in Australia is that a goal or is it not really an issue, to sound American and what would that mean anyway?

That’s a whole other topic of discussion that’s very complex. I think, because it’s tricky isn’t it, because fundamentally this is American music and jazz will always be American. I mean it’s such a huge cultural gift to the world, this music, but of course jazz at the same time it’s malleable. You know you can bring other influences into it. It can be fused © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

with Cuban or whatever. I mean, you know, jazz is something that is welcoming to other styles and it turns into something new but I think it will always be fundamentally American. There are some jazz organizations in Australia, kind of contemporary jazz organizations, and rather than use the word “jazz” they say “improvised music.” So they kind of — glibly they’re kind of detaching themselves from the tradition of American music. They’re saying hey, we’re making this our own, so it becomes more improvisation based, more original music based, and certainly a lot of the stuff that people compose in Australia is less swing orientated and more straight-eighth orientated or world music influences is a big movement for that. So there’s a movement for contemporary music to be away from jazz in Australia, it’s like let’s not call this jazz, this is not American music, now it’s “improvised music.” So you know there’s a lot of factors to it. There’s the traditionalists that really love the American music and the history of it, and there’s cats in Australia that study really all the recordings and they know their business and they play American. I don’t know what that means. But I think you know yeah, it’s complicated. What do you think?

I’m fascinated by — I second your thoughts about jazz and I think that America’s most important export has been its music starting with blues and jazz and rock & roll and hip hop, and the spread of it around the country is amazing. You know you can listen to music from South Korea that sounds like hip hop, it’s just that they’re singing in Korean. So I guess popular music has been extremely influenced by American music around the world and I guess that’s the best I can think. I’m fascinated by some of those stories way back in the late twenties when they were recording and they couldn’t record the drums because it made the stylus fall off the wax so they used a woodblock instead and then the French musicians were copying that and so they used a woodblock because that’s what they heard. I think that stuff is just so fascinating.
Yeah. There’s a touch of folklore to that, isn’t there.
